title: Service Level Objectives
subtitle: Define what users experience, the target, and any contractual consequence
summary: Pip’s backend is fast, yet the booking page remains unusable. Indicators need a defined population and measurement point; objectives need user-relevant targets. The crew separates engineering goals from contractual consequences and checks latency tails as well as averages.

concepts.title: Service level indicators
concepts.body: Pip’s backend timer says fast while the passenger cannot complete a booking. An SLI quantitatively describes success, latency, or another service property. Its definition states what, where, which population, and which interval are measured. Pip documents exclusions and measures close enough to the user to capture the actual experience.

concepts.title: Service level objectives
concepts.body: Pip stares at a latency histogram without knowing whether to act. An SLO sets a target or acceptable range for a defined SLI. A goal might require 99% of eligible responses within 400 milliseconds over a specified window. Pip chooses a few meaningful workload-sensitive objectives, refining them instead of promising the best performance ever observed.

concepts.title: Agreements and consequences
concepts.body: Pip calls an internal response target a customer contract. An SLA includes agreed consequences for service commitments; an SLO can guide engineering without one. SRE helps make commitments measurable and feasible, while business and legal participants decide contractual consequences. Pip distinguishes a service-credit agreement from an internal goal or reputational concern.

concepts.title: Distributions and expectations
concepts.body: Pip celebrates a stable median while the 99th percentile worsens. Averages hide minority experiences; percentiles expose parts of the distribution. Pip checks sampling and aggregation windows before comparing results. Clients can still break while a service meets its objective if they relied on better observed behavior than the promise.

misconceptions.claim: A low average latency proves almost every request is fast.
misconceptions.correction: A slow tail can coexist with an unchanged mean; inspect the latency distribution.

misconceptions.claim: A service without a customer SLA does not need SLOs.
misconceptions.correction: Internal objectives still guide engineering priorities and clarify expected behavior.

scenario.title: Define the customer-visible target
scenario.context: A search service reports thousands of internal metrics, but users complain about slow results at the tail. Product, SRE, and support need a target for the next quarter.

options.label: Choose a latency SLI and percentile SLO
options.benefit: The target represents user experience and creates a useful decision signal.
options.cost: Instrumentation and percentile selection require careful work.
options.consequence: The team chooses a p95 result latency over a rolling window and reviews misses.

options.label: Start with availability SLO
options.benefit: It is easier to measure and gives users a clear reliability floor.
options.cost: It may miss the tail-latency complaint that motivated the work.
options.consequence: The team protects basic availability first, then adds a latency SLI when it can define the user journey.

scenario.debrief: Availability-first measurement is a reasonable floor under limited instrumentation, but it leaves the slow-results journey unmeasured and must be extended deliberately.

quiz.question: Which statement defines an SLO rather than just an SLI?
options: The 99th percentile latency measured at the client
99% of eligible client requests finish within 400 ms each day
A refund is due when the contract is breached
quiz.explanation: The statement combines a defined service measure with a target and period.

quiz.question: Backend responses are fast, but a page remains unusable for seconds. Which measurement best addresses this gap?
options: The count of successful TCP connections
Client-side time until the page is usable
quiz.explanation: The user’s experience includes work after the backend has responded.

quiz.question: What distinguishes an SLA from an internal SLO?
options: Consequences attached to the service agreement
A target written with more decimal places
A percentile instead of an average
quiz.explanation: An agreement specifies consequences; an objective by itself specifies desired behavior.

exercise.title: Specify a measurable promise
exercise.prompt: Write one search-latency objective that another team could implement without guessing. Distinguish its measurement from any contractual consequence.
